To enfeeble something or someone means to make it weak, frail, or less capable than it was before. When something enfeebles a person or a thing, it strips away strength, power, or vitality — leaving behind a diminished, fragile version of what once existed.

Think of a once-vigorous athlete who, after a prolonged illness, struggles to even walk across a room. That illness has enfeebled them. The strength they had is gone, replaced by frailty and helplessness.

This is important: enfeeble does not mean merely tired or temporarily drained. It describes a more serious, often lasting reduction in capacity. Something that has been enfeebled is genuinely and significantly diminished — it has lost its vigour, its robustness, its ability to function as it once did.

There is also always a cause behind the weakening. Something actively does the enfeebling — a disease, a force, a policy, a circumstance. The weakness doesn't arise on its own; it is inflicted or brought about.

This word is remarkably versatile. It can apply to people, institutions, systems, and even abstract things like ideas or arguments.

A person physically: A long famine had so thoroughly enfeebled the survivors that many couldn't stand without support.

A person mentally: The years of isolation slowly enfeebled his mind, making it difficult for him to think clearly or retain memories.

An institution or government: Decades of corruption have enfeebled the judiciary, hollowing out its authority until it can no longer deliver justice.

A nation or economy: The prolonged civil war enfeebled the country beyond any quick recovery.

An argument or idea: Every compromise they made further enfeebled their position, until their original point had lost all its force.

So whether it is a human body, a mind, a system of government, or even a line of reasoning — all of these can be enfeebled.
How the verb works in a sentence

Enfeeble is a transitive verb, which means it always needs two things: something doing the enfeebling (the cause), and something being enfeebled (the target).

The prolonged grief enfeebled her. — Grief is the cause; she is the target.

Years of underfunding have enfeebled the public health system. — Underfunding is the cause; the health system is the target.

It is also very commonly used in the passive voice, where the focus shifts to what happened to the target rather than who caused it:

He was enfeebled by age and sorrow.

The institution has been enfeebled over decades of neglect.

Enfeeble is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual conversation — nobody says "I'm feeling a bit enfeebled today" over breakfast. It lives in serious writing: essays, literary fiction, historical accounts, formal journalism, or academic texts.

When a writer reaches for "enfeeble" instead of a simpler word like "weaken," they are usually trying to convey something weightier — a deeper, more dramatic, or more permanent loss of strength. The word carries a gravity that plain alternatives don't always have.
How it compares to similar words

Placing enfeeble among its neighbours makes its meaning sharper.

Weaken is the broad, everyday version. Enfeeble is more formal and more specific — it implies not just reduced strength, but genuine frailty and vulnerability.

Debilitate is close and is often used in medical settings to describe physical incapacity: a debilitating injury, a debilitating condition. Enfeeble can extend more naturally into non-physical territory like institutions or ideas.

Enervate means to drain someone of energy or vitality — "the relentless heat enervated the soldiers." It tends to have a mental or emotional flavour. Enfeeble, by contrast, stresses the resulting frailty more than the draining process itself.

Undermine means to erode something from within, often gradually and insidiously. You undermine confidence, authority, or a structure. Enfeeble is more direct — it simply makes something weak, without the hidden or subversive flavour of "undermine."

Sap means to slowly drain strength away — "the long siege sapped the army's morale." It suggests a gradual, draining process. Enfeeble is more formal and emphasises the resulting weakened state more than the gradual process of getting there.

Incapacitate is stronger than enfeeble. An incapacitated person is entirely unable to function. An enfeebled person is weakened and fragile, but not necessarily completely out of action.

Enfeebles (present): Chronic stress enfeebles the immune system over time.

Enfeebled (past tense / adjective): The enfeebled king handed his crown to his son. / Years of poverty had enfeebled the entire community.

Enfeebling (ongoing action): The enfeebling effects of the drought were felt across the whole region.

To enfeeble is to make someone or something significantly weaker, more frail, and less capable — and this weakening is always caused by something, whether it is disease, neglect, hardship, or any other force that drains away strength and vitality.
